strengths: Novel and well-motivated formalization: the paper defines multi-agent systems as labeled DAGs with communication/CoT edges grounded in UHAT expressivity, cleanly extending prior single-agent CoT theory (Amiri et al., 2025) to the multi-agent setting — a gap not addressed by prior expressivity work or by PRAM/MPC-style analyses that ignore agent computation limits.

Clean theoretical structure: three distinct depth-communication regimes are identified, each instantiated by a naturalistic task (associative recall, state tracking over finite monoids, k-hop reasoning), with matching upper and lower bounds (e.g., Prop. 4.1 size conservation, Prop. 4.2 impossibility of the fourth regime, Prop. 4.7 optimality for state tracking).

Theory-practice bridge: the paper convincingly connects each theoretical regime to existing applied multi-agent systems (CoA, LLM×MapReduce, NexusSum, etc.) and derives actionable design guidance (prefix-sum cascade vs. single manager, iterative query for multi-hop).

Empirical validation is aligned with the theory: experiments on Llama-70B/8B/EXAONE with controlled synthetic benchmarks confirm predicted accuracy trends and the depth-communication Pareto tradeoff for the prefix-sum protocol.

Good reproducibility: full codebase, detailed prompts, hyperparameters, and ablations (branching factor) are provided; the appendix contains complete proofs and thorough clarifications addressing scope questions (LRMs, shared-context protocols, debate/voting).
weaknesses: The practical gap between theory and experiments is substantial: the theory covers idealized UHAT constructions with hard-coded communication and deterministic message passing, while experiments use prompted pretrained LLMs with empirical failure modes (instruction drift, hallucination). The paper acknowledges this but does not quantify how tightly the idealized bounds predict observed behavior.

Several theoretical results are conceptually expected: the state tracking speedup is essentially the classical parallel prefix-sum/scan algorithm lifted into the multi-agent graph framework, and the size lower bound for PARITY follows directly from prior single-agent results (Amiri et al. 2025) via Proposition 4.1; the novelty lies more in the framework than in deep new proof techniques.

Some optimality claims rest on weak or informal arguments: the depth lower bound in Prop. C.7 is a corollary of size conservation (which holds only up to a constant factor), the k-hop depth optimality is only up to a log(N+k) factor with a somewhat informal worst-case argument, and assumptions (contiguous disjoint partitioning, optimal-communication-budget families) limit the generality of the lower bounds.

Empirical evaluation is limited in scale and baselines: only two to three protocol baselines (majority voting, CoA), small synthetic task sizes (e.g., PARITY up to 512 bits, k-hop up to 20 hops/500 facts), 100 runs per configuration, and no evaluation on real benchmarks or realistic long-context tasks — the practical significance of the recommended protocols (e.g., prefix-sum cascade) remains untested outside the synthetic setting.

Certain empirical claims are weakly supported: Figure 5(c) depth-vs-hops is partly a consequence of the protocol's own O(k) round structure, and the depth-communication plot for PARITY shows deviations at high communication that the paper attributes to instruction-following noise without deeper analysis.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('outpts', duplicated case (ii) in Definition 3.1), an incomplete reproducibility URL in the statement, and informal passages in proofs (e.g., asynchronous communication handling in Prop. C.5) that would benefit from tightening.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated question: formalizing communication and resource tradeoffs in multi-agent LLM reasoning, connecting the Transformer expressivity literature (Hahn; Merrill & Sabharwal; Amiri et al.; Jerad et al.) to an applied area that currently lacks theoretical grounding.

Clean formalization (Definition 3.1/3.2/3.3) of multi-agent systems as labeled DAGs with CoT and communication edges, with sensible complexity measures (depth, width, size, communication budget) that map onto wall-clock time, parallelism, and token cost.

The paper provides essentially matching upper and lower bounds for state tracking (O(log w + N/w) depth, Θ(w) communication, Ω(N) size via Amiri et al.), a clean impossibility result (Prop 4.2) ruling out one regime, and a three-regime taxonomy that is instantiated by concrete naturalistic tasks.

Empirical validation on synthetic tasks broadly shows the predicted behaviors: prefix-sum cascades outperform chain-of-agents/majority voting on PARITY and S5 permutation tracking, and the depth-communication tradeoff curves qualitatively follow the theory.

Good discussion connecting the framework to PRAM/MPC/LOCAL models, explaining why modeling agents as Transformers (rather than RAM processors) yields qualitatively different and more LLM-relevant predictions; reproducibility package with prompts and details is provided.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core technical constructions. The key upper bounds are classical techniques repackaged: parallel prefix-sum/scan for state tracking, induction-head constructions for associative recall (essentially Bhattamishra et al. 2024), and iterative lookup for k-hop. The main new content is the multi-agent formalism and the taxonomy, which is partly trivial: the impossibility regime follows directly from Prop 4.2, and the depth lower bound Ω(N/w) is an immediate corollary of size conservation.

Several lower-bound arguments are informal or only hold in restrictive settings: the k-hop communication lower bound Ω(k) is argued via a w=2 reduction to Tesson–Thérien with a hand-wavy extension to larger w, and depth optimality is only claimed 'up to a log(N+k) factor' and only in the worst case over fact distributions; the model assumes all agents share the same Transformer parameters, fresh contexts per communication round, and hard-coded communication scheduling, which weakens the connection to real multi-agent systems.

The empirical section is narrow and does not really test the theory's distinctive claims. All experiments are tiny synthetic tasks (parity, S5 with ≤16 swaps, k-hop with ≤500 facts) on two/three instruct LLMs, with hard-coded communication; no evaluation on any real multi-agent benchmark or task from the applied literature the paper claims to inform. The anomalous spikes in the depth-vs-communication plots (Fig 4b, 6, 14) are attributed to 'poor instruction following' rather than analyzed.

The framework deliberately excludes broad classes of multi-agent systems (self-consistency/debate with shared input, GroupThink-style shared contexts, LRMs), yet these are arguably the most common real paradigms; the scope restriction is acknowledged but limits the significance of the 'guidance for designing scalable multi-agent systems' claim.

Significance of the three-regime result is modest: the finding that some tasks parallelize (state tracking), some need no communication (recall), and some need Θ(k) communication (k-hop) is largely predictable from known circuit/communication-complexity intuitions and prior single-agent CoT results; the paper does not identify any surprising separation.

Presentation problems: a broken sentence in the Reproducibility Statement (URL missing), typos ('outpts', 'self-consistencty', 'consequent with'), inconsistent notation across propositions (w vs k as number-of-agents argument in k-hop tradeoffs), and Table 1's communication column for k-hop mixes Θ/optimality claims that only hold conditionally (w > 1).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored question: the formal expressive capacity of multi-agent LLM reasoning systems. Extending the CoT-expressivity literature (Merrill & Sabharwal; Amiri et al.) to a multi-agent communication setting is a genuine and meaningful contribution.

The formalization (Def. 3.1-3.3) is clean and general: multi-agent systems as labeled DAGs with communication and CoT edges, with well-defined notions of depth, width, size, and communication budget. The framework is shown to cover a broad class of applied multi-agent systems (CoA, LLM×MapReduce, LongAgent, XpandA, etc.), which strengthens the practical relevance of the theory.

The characterization of three depth-communication regimes (Table 2) is elegant, and the paper proves that the fourth regime is impossible (Prop. 4.2), giving the result a completeness that goes beyond mere protocol cataloging.

For each of the three task families the authors provide essentially matching upper and lower bounds (e.g., Θ(w) communication and Ω(N/w) depth for state tracking over nontrivial groups; Θ(k) communication for k-hop reasoning via a communication-complexity argument based on permutation composition). The proofs in Appendix C build carefully on established constructions (J-L vectors, prefix sums, threshold-circuit-to-MLP simulations).

Empirical validation is well-designed relative to the theory: the authors implement the provably optimal protocols (Prefix Sum, Iterative Query) and compare against natural baselines (Majority Voting, Chain-of-Agents) across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, EXAONE) and tasks, with ablations over branching factors showing the predicted depth-communication Pareto frontier.

The clarifications appendix (Section B) proactively addresses scope questions (no LRM experiments, same-input protocols like debate/voting, unbounded-communication settings) honestly and convincingly, and a reproducibility package with prompts and experimental details is provided.
weaknesses: The theoretical model assumes unique hard attention (UHAT), single-token messages, disjoint input partitioning, and synchronous decoding with fresh contexts per round. These are significant simplifications relative to practical multi-agent LLM systems; the bridge from UHAT theory to actual soft-attention LLMs is asserted rather than established, so the 'plausibility' of the model rests largely on prior work rather than on evidence in this paper.

Several optimality claims are looser than the abstract suggests: the k-hop depth lower bound holds only up to a log(N+k) factor and relies on a somewhat informal worst-case argument (two-agent distribution of relevant facts); the depth upper bound for state tracking is optimal only up to an O(log w(N)) factor. The main text's phrasing ('essentially optimal') occasionally overstates the precision of the results.

The core constructions (prefix sums / parallel scans for associative-composition tasks, iterative lookup for chained retrieval) are classical results from parallel and distributed algorithms; the novelty lies in their translation into UHAT multi-agent systems rather than in fundamentally new algorithmic ideas. Reviewers steeped in MPC/PRAM theory may find the contribution more incremental than the framing suggests.

The empirical validation is confined to small-scale synthetic tasks with hard-coded communication topologies. It confirms that LLMs can execute the prescribed protocols and that coarse trends match theory, but it does not test whether the theory predicts performance of realistic, adaptive multi-agent systems on natural tasks (acknowledged as future work). Some measured trends (e.g., slight depth increases in high-communication regimes) deviate from predictions and are only qualitatively explained.

The framework explicitly excludes same-input protocols (debate, self-consistency ensembles, GroupThink-style shared context), which constitute a large fraction of the multi-agent LLM literature; the claimed 'broad applicability' therefore needs qualification.

Minor presentation issues: the reproduction statement contains an incomplete sentence (missing URL); there are typos (e.g., 'self-consistencty', 'outpts', 'the each agent'); Table 1's Depth entry for state tracking (O(N/w + log w)) vs. the text's O(log w + N/w) notation is inconsistent; Definition 3.1 item 4 has duplicated enumeration '(ii)'.

The distinction between the paper's contribution and existing single-agent CoT lower bounds (e.g., Prop. 4.4 reduces directly to Amiri et al.'s Ω(N) CoT bound) is thin in places; the genuinely new content is concentrated in the upper-bound protocols and the communication-budget lower bounds.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned question: formalizing when communication provably helps in multi-agent LLM reasoning, extending the recent line of Transformer expressivity work (e.g., Amiri et al. 2025, Merrill & Sabharwal) to multi-agent settings — this gap is real and timely.

Clean formal framework (Definition 3.1/3.2) that abstracts practical systems (Chain-of-Agents, LLM×MapReduce, LongAgent, etc.) with explicit mapping to applied literature in Section 3.1 and Appendix B.

Concrete, mostly matching upper and lower bounds: three regimes for depth/communication instantiated by natural tasks (associative recall Θ(1)/Θ(1), state tracking O(log w + N/w) with Θ(w) communication, k-hop reasoning Θ(k)/Θ(k)), plus a size-conservation argument that rules out a fourth regime.

Interesting separation result (Prop. H.1) showing a super-polynomial gap between majority voting and PrefixSum for PARITY at matched computation depth, leveraging circuit complexity results (Aspnes et al., 1991) — this goes beyond prior conjecture-based comparisons (Mirtaheri et al., 2025).

Technical proofs are substantive: explicit UHAT constructions using Johnson-Lindenstrauss embeddings, induction-head retrieval, threshold-circuit-to-MLP conversions; error analysis of the parity tree (Appendix D) connects theory to practice.

Empirical validation on pretrained LLMs (Llama-8B/70B, EXAONE) across three tasks broadly corroborates the theoretically predicted regimes and depth–communication tradeoffs, with sensible baselines (majority voting, CoA) and ablations; reproducibility package with full prompts is provided.

Thoughtful appendix addressing scope limitations (multi-token messages, voting/debate paradigms, fixed-precision soft attention) including a transfer argument to finite-precision softmax Transformers.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty in the core algorithms: the state-tracking upper bounds are essentially a parallel prefix-scan / divide-and-conquer composition over an associative monoid — a classic PRAM result (Blelloch scan) — instantiated in the LLM setting; the surprise value of the 'three regimes' taxonomy is therefore moderate.

Several lower bounds are informal or rely on heuristic arguments: the Ω(w(N)) communication lower bound in Prop. 4.7/C.7 rests on the assertion 'each agent must send at least one message' without a rigorous proof, and the depth lower bound follows from the size-conservation inequality, whose proof sketch assumes inputs must be partitioned; the k-hop depth bound is only up to a log(N+k) factor.

The empirical setting is narrow: only synthetic, controlled tasks with near-ideal protocol implementations; no evaluation on realistic multi-agent workloads (long-document QA, summarization) where the theory would be most useful, and 'computation depth' is only proxied by token usage, creating some theory–experiment mismatch acknowledged by the authors (instruction-following overhead).

The framework assumes disjoint contiguous input partitioning with bounded per-step communication; popular paradigms such as debate, self-consistency, and shared-context architectures (e.g., GroupThink) fall outside the model, limiting the claimed breadth of 'multi-agent reasoning systems'.

Experiments use relatively small problem sizes (parity up to length 512, k-hop up to 20 hops) where asymptotic predictions are only weakly distinguishable; the worst-case claims (e.g., error compounding toward 1/2 for PARITY) are not stress-tested at scale.

Writing quality issues: minor typos ('outpts', doubled punctuation, malformed citation in Prop. C.4), a broken/empty code URL in the Reproducibility Statement, and some mislabeled references (Figure 1(c) caption points to the wrong section).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question: formalizing expressivity of multi-agent LLM reasoning with communication, extending the UHAT/CoT expressivity literature (Merrill & Sabharwal, Amiri et al.) to a multi-agent setting with a clean graph-based formalization.

The organization of results into three regimes (no communication gain, depth-communication tradeoff, unavoidable communication) is a nice conceptual contribution, and the claim that all three regimes are instantiated by natural tasks is well supported by the theory (Prop. 4.3, 4.6, 4.8).

Several results include matching or near-matching upper and lower bounds (e.g., optimal communication budget for state tracking and k-hop reasoning), and the super-polynomial separation between PrefixSum and majority voting (Prop. H.1) using voting-polynomial lower bounds (Aspnes et al., 1991) is a nontrivial and interesting result.

Positioning relative to parallel computing frameworks (PRAM, BSP, LOCAL, communication complexity) is thoughtful, and the appendix clarifications (App. B, G, H, I) are unusually thorough, addressing fixed-precision transformers, multi-token messages, and voting schemes.

The empirical section implements the theory-predicted protocols with pretrained LLMs and reports trends (accuracy, computation depth vs. communication) broadly consistent with theoretical predictions; reproducibility materials, prompts, and hyperparameter details are provided.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core technical insights: the main upper-bound constructions (parallel prefix-scan/scan for associative operations, iterative sequential lookup for k-hop chains) are textbook parallel/distributed algorithms; the contribution is mainly transplanting them into the UHAT framework rather than new techniques. A knowledgeable reader will find the direction of the results unsurprising.

Some optimality claims are weaker than advertised: the depth lower bound for state tracking (Prop. 4.7) follows directly from the trivial size inequality (2) and gives only N/w(N); the k-hop depth lower bound holds only up to a log(N+k) factor and only in a specially constructed worst case. Several Θ labels in Table 1 rely on these partial optimality results.

The empirical validation is confined to synthetic tasks (parity, needle-in-a-haystack, S5 swaps, synthetic k-hop facts) with hard-coded communication protocols, so the central empirical claim — that 'communication is provably beneficial' in practice — is largely baked into the experimental design rather than tested on realistic multi-agent workloads or learned behavior. The gap between the idealized UHAT model and prompted API agents is acknowledged but not quantified.

Experiments use only two main model families (Llama-8B/70B, EXAONE in appendix), mostly small-scale regimes (N up to ~2^11 for parity), and some key quantities (e.g., computation depth measured via token usage as a proxy) are noisy proxies whose agreement with theory is qualitative at best.

Practical significance is modest: the paper's own design implications (prefix-sum cascade, iterative manager-worker querying) are proposed but not implemented or evaluated as methods; the majority-voting lower bound concerns exact, error-free computation, which the authors concede may not extend to realistic accuracy regimes.

Presentation quality is uneven: several typos and grammatical slips ('outpts', 'each each', 'consequent with', double period in conclusion, malformed enumeration in Def. 3.1 item 4), and Proposition 6.1 is labeled informal while the formal version is deferred to an appendix; the main text at times oversells optimality ('proves it optimal') relative to what the proofs establish.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed research question: the paper formalizes, for the first time in a principled way, the expressivity and communication tradeoffs of multi-agent LLM reasoning systems, extending the established UHAT/CoT expressivity literature (Merrill & Sabharwal; Amiri et al.) to the multi-agent setting.

Clean, general formalization (Definition 3.1/3.2/3.3) of multi-agent systems as labeled DAGs with CoT and communication edges, with cost measures (size, width, depth, communication budget) that map naturally onto practical quantities (total compute, wall-clock time, context bottlenecks).

Strong theoretical results: matching upper and lower bounds for three natural task families (associative recall, state tracking over monoids, k-hop reasoning), yielding a crisp three-regime taxonomy plus an impossibility result (Prop. 4.2). The optimality results (e.g., Θ(w) communication and Ω(N/w) depth for state tracking) are non-trivial and well-supported by detailed constructions in the appendix.

A valuable and technically interesting separation result (Appendix H): a super-polynomial gap between prefix-sum cascades and majority-voting/self-consistency schemes for PARITY, leveraging voting-polynomial lower bounds (Aspnes et al., 1991) — this directly connects theory to widely used practical baselines.

Empirical validation is thoughtfully designed: hardcoded implementations of the theoretically optimal protocols on real LLMs (Llama-8B/70B, EXAONE) across three tasks, showing that accuracy and token-usage/computation-depth tradeoffs align with the theoretical predictions. Ablations over branching factors, chunk sizes, and agent counts support the Pareto-frontier claims.

Excellent positioning and discussion: clear connections to PRAM/BSP/LOCAL/communication complexity, and to applied multi-agent systems (CoA, LLM×MapReduce, LongAgent, XpandA, etc.). The clarifications appendix anticipates reviewer concerns (why no LRMs, why no voting/debate, why single-token messages) with substantive, honest answers.
Good reproducibility: complete proofs, full prompts, hyperparameters, and a stated reproducibility package.
weaknesses: The framework restricts to disjoint input partitioning and point-to-point/broadcast single-token messages; protocols like multi-agent debate or shared-context systems (e.g., GroupThink) fall outside the model. While this is acknowledged and justified, it limits the scope of the conclusions for the broader multi-agent ecosystem.

The theory assumes all agents share a single UHAT Transformer, and UHAT itself is an idealization; although Appendix I argues transfers to fixed-precision softmax transformers, the gap between the abstract model and real autoregressive LLM agents (with stochastic decoding and imperfect instruction following) is only bridged empirically, not formally.

The experimental evaluation is limited in scale and diversity: synthetic tasks (PARITY, needle-in-a-haystack, S5 swaps, k-hop facts), two-to-three API models, and hardcoded deterministic communication protocols. Practical impact of the proposed cascade/iterative-query designs is asserted as future work rather than demonstrated on realistic workloads.

Depth optimality for k-hop reasoning is only up to a log(N+k) factor, and the parity-tree error analysis (Appendix D) shows error probabilities approach 1/2 asymptotically for the prefix-sum protocol under per-node error, a caveat that weakens the 'optimal protocol' framing in noisy real-model settings.

Some minor presentation issues: typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'outpts' in Prop. C.1 proof, 'each each' in Appendix D, formatting in Def. 3.1 item 4, an apparent typo '2N/w' vs '2N+1' in the Appendix C.4 construction), and the mismatch between Prop. 4.6 (O(N) size) and Table 1 entries could confuse readers.

The empirical 'computation depth' is proxied by token usage, which the authors themselves note is confounded by instruction-following overhead in high-communication regimes; a more direct wall-clock measurement would strengthen the validation.
